practical.title: Module 2.2 — Structs and a Linked List: Implementing insert_at_end
practical.sourceActivity: Module 2.2 — Structs and a Linked List: Implementing insert_at_end

coachingPrompts: What do you predict will happen before you run it?
What evidence shows that your change worked?
Can you explain the result in your own words?

files.description: Runnable C starter file for the practical.

tasks.title: Observe & Understand — run the baseline program
tasks.narratorGuide: Start by compiling and running the supplied main.c exactly as provided. Observe the three printed lines: the list after head insertions, the list after end insertions, and the empty-list test. The program compiles and runs but shows that end insertions did not change the main list — a classic sign that the new node was created but not linked to the last node. Understanding that difference (creating memory vs. linking pointers) is crucial. Next you'll make a minimal correction so that the list actually links the new tail. Keep an eye on the bug comment in the code: that's your clue.

tasks.title: Modify & Experiment — one-line fix to link the new node
tasks.narratorGuide: Now edit main.c: locate the insert_at_end function and replace the single line current = new_node; with current->next = new_node;. This changes a local pointer reassignment into an update of the previous node's next field — the essential step for linking. Save, recompile, and run. You should now see the main list grows to include 40 and 50. This small edit demonstrates how pointer target updates (not pointer variable reassignments) change data structure shape.

tasks.title: Build & Integrate — experiment by adding more end insertions
tasks.narratorGuide: Add two insert_at_end calls after the existing ones to append 60 and 70. This is a small integration test: if the function maintains the tail correctly, repeated calls should extend the list in order. Also try calling insert_at_end on a NULL head (we already do that for empty_list_head); that single-case was already handled by returning new_node. Recompile and run to confirm results. This step solidifies confidence that the function behaves for both empty and non-empty lists.

tasks.title: Verify & Extend — add a node counter and verify counts
tasks.narratorGuide: Add and compile a small count_nodes function that returns how many nodes a list contains. In main, after your insertions, print the counts for the main list and the empty_list_head. This is precise verification — printed counts make it trivial to assert correctness (for example, after 3 head inserts and 4 end inserts you should see 7). Finally, think about the next extension: if append performance matters, wrap head and tail in a List struct to make append O(1). That's a good advanced exercise.

safety.learnerWarning: This practical runs in an isolated workspace. Do not use real credentials or production resources.
